analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending at $200,000, slashes PAC contribution limits, and gives taxpayers a credit for small donations.
analysis.headline: A House campaign-finance bill limiting spending and PAC money was referred to four committees and three subcommittees and died without ever reaching a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let House candidates voluntarily accept a $200,000 spending cap, with only $50,000 of their own money allowed, in exchange for cheaper TV and radio time and half-price campaign mail. It would have cut the limit on PAC contributions from $5,000 to $1,000 per election, barred most PAC money above $100,000 per election cycle, banned candidate-controlled political committees, and stopped candidates from spending campaign funds personally. It also offered every taxpayer a tax credit of up to $100 ($200 for couples) for small donations to qualifying House candidates, and required TV ads paid for by outside groups to name their sponsor continuously on screen. The bill never got past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want campaigns less dependent on big checks: small donors would get a dollar-for-dollar tax credit of up to $100 for contributing to qualifying House candidates in their own district; candidates without personal wealth or PAC pipelines would get cheaper advertising and mail; viewers would see who is really paying for political ads.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, small donors, and underfunded challengers

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who sign up get a $200,000 spending cap per election, including a hard $50,000 cap on their own personal funds, aimed at campaigns financed by the candidate's own wealth

The limit on what a multicandidate PAC can give any candidate drops from $5,000 to $1,000 per election, and House candidates may accept no more than $100,000 total ($125,000 in some cases) from nonparty PACs per election cycle
Every individual could claim a tax credit of up to $100 per year ($200 on joint returns) for contributions to qualifying House candidates, effectively making small donations free to the donor

Candidates cannot use campaign money for personal purposes and cannot control political committees other than their own authorized committee, closing a channel for converting donations to private benefit

Independent-expenditure TV ads must show their sponsor's name continuously on screen, and outside ads must disclose that their cost is not subject to contribution limits, plus a provision foreshadowing 'stand by your ad': candidate ads must state the candidate reviewed and approved them

Qualifying candidates get reduced postal rates (half-price first-class and qualified-political-committee third-class rates) for mail sent in the 90 days before an election, and stations that willfully discriminate against candidates can lose their FCC license

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees, which would see their per-candidate limit cut 80% and their total allowed giving to a House campaign capped; broadcast stations, which would face published election-period rates, a priority-access duty, and license revocation for discriminating against candidates; wealthy self-financing candidates, who would have to give up spending above $50,000 of their own money to qualify; and the Treasury, which would forgo revenue on the donation tax credit.

drawbacks.text: The spending limits are voluntary and porous: if a non-participating candidate spends more than 50% over the $200,000 cap, the cap lifts for everyone in the race, so the restrictions only hold when both sides accept them
The bill does not touch independent expenditures — outside groups could still spend without limit on behalf of candidates, subject only to stronger disclosure

A flat $200,000 cap is a one-size-fits-all number that could seriously handicap candidates in expensive media markets, and its ratemaking carve-out lets newspapers and magazines give qualifying candidates discounted advertising without it counting as a contribution
The tax credit costs the Treasury revenue and relies on donors' signed self-attestation of contributions, with no recipient identification required on the claim

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: candidates give up huge war chests in exchange for cheaper airtime, cheaper mail, and public financing through the tax credit, which would have made small-dollar donors matter more and PAC money matter less. The voluntary trigger and the untouched independent-expenditure channel are genuine weaknesses, and a $200,000 cap may be too low in big-media-market districts — but on balance the bill attacked the money-in-politics problem directly, and the costs fall on the concentrated interests that benefit from the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House sent it to four committees at once, they passed it down to three subcommittees and asked federal agencies for comments, and no committee ever reported it out before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Pease (D-OH) introduced the bill on May 2, 1989 as comprehensive campaign reform for House elections
The same day, the House referred it jointly to four committees: House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Post Office and Civil Service, and Ways and Means

In May 1989 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Elections, the Subcommittee on Postal Operations and Services, and the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, and executive comments were requested from OMB, the Postal Service, and the FEC
On June 22, 1989 the FEC was asked for its comments; that was the last action ever recorded on the bill
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote occurred, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill dead

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing campaign money system's biggest participants came out ahead: political action committees kept the $5,000 per-election limit and uncapped aggregate giving, broadcasters kept discretion over candidate rates and access, and wealthy self-funding candidates kept unlimited personal spending. Incumbents running for reelection in 1990 never had to vote on it.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, passed it to the Subcommittee on Elections, and never reported it out

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the broadcast-related title on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, and never reported it out

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached the floor, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, but only four of 257 House Democrats supported it in any visible way.

industries.note: The bill cuts the PAC per-election contribution limit from $5,000 to $1,000, caps total nonparty PAC money to a House candidate at $100,000 per cycle, bars PACs from backing multiple candidates in one general election, and lets donors earmark their PAC contributions. PACs' ability to aggregate and steer organized money would shrink sharply, which is the point from the voter's side.

Stations would have to publish their election-period rates in advance, give qualified candidates priority access, and could lose their FCC license for willfully discriminating against a candidate. This trades away broadcaster discretion over campaign airtime and rates for guaranteed candidate access.

Qualifying candidates could spend no more than $50,000 of their own money per election, the first real brake on campaigns bought with personal fortunes. Spending past the trigger by a non-qualifying rival would void the cap for everyone, but the default rule would be a cap.

The bill expressly excludes advertising rate reductions that newspapers and magazines give to qualifying House candidates from the definition of a campaign contribution, so publishers could offer discounted ads that never count against any limit. It is a targeted carve-out for print media inside a bill otherwise built on tightening money rules.

Qualifying candidates would mail campaign material at half the first-class rate and at third-class political rates during the final 90 days, reducing postal revenue. The lost revenue is the price of cheaper campaign mail for candidates who accept limits.
